code: ## 3. Per-Cell Quality Control Metrics  Quality control (QC) is a critical first step in any single cell analysis. The goal is to identify and remove low-quality cells that could confound downstream analysis. Here, we calculate four key metrics for each cell:  1. **nCount_RNA**: The total number of UMI counts (library size) 2. **nFeature_RNA**: The number of genes detected 3. **percent.mt**: The percentage of counts from mitochondrial genes 4. **percent.ribo**: The percentage of counts from ribosomal genes  Cells with very few genes detected are likely empty droplets or debris. Conversely, cells with unusually high counts may represent doublets. High mitochondrial content often indicates cell stress or death, as damaged cells leak cytoplasmic RNA while retaining mitochondrial RNA.  ```{r qc-metrics} # High mitochondrial content indicates cell stress or death seurat[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(seurat, pattern = "^MT-")  # Ribosomal genes are highly expressed but not informative for cell typing seurat[["percent.ribo"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(seurat, pattern = "^RP[SL]")

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Quality control (QC) critical first step single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. goal QC identify remove low-quality cells confound downstream analysis. Poor quality cells can arise several sources: empty droplets contain ambient RNA, dying cells compromised membranes, doublets two cells captured single droplet. module, work single nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) data human heart tissue. data comes study examining human heart development across three stages: foetal, young, adult (Sim et al., 2021, Circulation). Understanding heart changes cellular level across development provides insights cardiac maturation potential therapeutic targets.

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Traditional “bulk” RNA-sequencing measures average gene expression across millions cells. powerful, approach masks heterogeneity exists within tissues. Single cell RNA-sequencing overcomes limitation measuring gene expression individual cells, allowing us : Identify distinct cell types within tissue Discover rare cell populations Study cell--cell variability Track cellular states development disease widely used platform scRNA-seq 10X Genomics Chromium system, captures cells oil droplets along barcoded beads. bead carries oligonucleotides three key components: Cell barcode: Identifies cell RNA came Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI): Identifies individual RNA molecules, removing PCR amplification bias Poly-dT tail: Captures polyadenylated mRNA

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Based QC visualisations established guidelines snRNA-seq data, define following filtering thresholds: Rationale threshold: min_genes = 500: Cells fewer genes likely empty droplets debris. 500-gene threshold commonly used snRNA-seq. min_counts = 2500: Ensures sufficient sequencing depth reliable downstream analysis. max_counts = 40000: Extremely high counts may indicate doublets escaped detection technical artefacts. max_mt = 20%: High mitochondrial content indicates cell stress death. 20% threshold appropriate snRNA-seq; scRNA-seq, 10% might suitable. singlets : Removes computationally identified doublets.
code: # Define filtering thresholds min_genes <- 500       # Minimum genes detected per cell min_counts <- 2500     # Minimum UMI counts per cell max_counts <- 40000    # Maximum UMI counts per cell max_mt <- 20           # Maximum mitochondrial percentage

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: remove four categories genes, specific reasons: 1. Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (~200 genes) genes nuclear genome encode proteins functioning within mitochondria (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins like MRPL20, MRPS15). expression correlates cellular metabolic state can confound biological comparisons. Note MT-prefixed genes (encoded mitochondrial genome ) already excluded data preprocessing. 2. Ribosomal protein genes (~190 genes) Ribosomal proteins (RPS RPL gene families) highly ubiquitously expressed across cell types. dominate variance calculations without providing useful biological insight distinguishing developmental disease-related transcriptional changes. 3. Genes without Entrez IDs (~9,000 genes) Genes lacking Entrez identifiers often pseudogenes, non-coding transcripts, poorly characterised sequences. Removing simplifies downstream functional annotation pathway analysis, Entrez IDs commonly required. 4. Sex chromosome genes (~800 genes) unbalanced sex distribution across developmental groups dataset (fetal: 2M/1F, young: 2M/1F, adult: 1M/2F), X Y chromosome genes may show spurious differential expression driven sample composition rather true developmental biology. Removing prevents confounding.

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: proceeding downstream analyses, informative examine sample-level relationships. aggregating (summing) counts across cells within sample, create “pseudobulk” expression profiles. allows us : Verify biological groups cluster together Identify potential batch effects Confirm biological signal dominates technical noise approach uses techniques traditional bulk RNA-seq analysis, well-established robust.
code: # Aggregate counts by sample # This sums all counts for each gene across all cells in each sample pseudobulk <- AggregateExpression(     seu_filtered,     group.by = "sample",     assays = "RNA",     return.seu = FALSE )$RNA  dim(pseudobulk) ## [1] 19001     9

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: use edgeR’s DGEList object store pseudobulk data perform filtering:
code: # Create DGEList object dge <- DGEList(counts = pseudobulk)  # Add sample information sample_info <- seu_filtered@meta.data %>%     dplyr::select(sample, group, sex) %>%     distinct() sample_info <- sample_info[match(colnames(dge), sample_info$sample), ]  dge$samples$group <- sample_info$group dge$samples$sex <- sample_info$sex  # Filter lowly expressed genes # This removes genes that don't have sufficient counts for reliable analysis keep <- filterByExpr(dge, group = dge$samples$group) dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]  # Calculate normalisation factors # This accounts for differences in library composition between samples dge <- calcNormFactors(dge)  dim(dge) ## [1] 16592     9

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: Normalisation one critical steps single cell analysis. Unlike bulk RNA-seq, samples similar total counts, single cells can vary orders magnitude total UMI counts due differences cell size, RNA content, capture efficiency. SCTransform (Hafemeister & Satija, 2019) uses regularised negative binomial regression normalise UMI count data. approach: Models relationship observed counts sequencing depth gene using negative binomial distribution Computes Pearson residuals represent deviation expected expression given sequencing depth Identifies genes high biological variability (variable features) drive downstream analyses key insight highly expressed genes show variance simply due sampling effects. SCTransform accounts modelling mean-variance relationship, allowing fair comparison across genes different expression levels. vst.flavor = "v2" option uses improved algorithm (Choudhary & Satija, 2022) : Uses geometric mean library size reference (robust) Implements improved regularisation better handling outliers Provides stable results large datasets SCTransform automatically identifies highly variable genes. Let us examine top variable features: can visualise mean-variance relationship:
code: # Run SCTransform normalisation # This may take 1-2 minutes set.seed(42)  # For reproducibility seu <- SCTransform(     seu,     vst.flavor = "v2",     seed.use = 42,     verbose = FALSE ) # Get the top 10 variable features top_features <- head(VariableFeatures(seu), 10) top_features ##  [1] "F13A1"     "NRXN1"     "ACSM3"     "CNTNAP2"   "XKR4"      "LINC02388" ##  [7] "KAZN"      "PKHD1L1"   "NEGR1"     "NRG1" # Plot variable features VariableFeaturePlot(seu) +     ggtitle("Variable Features (SCTransform)") +     theme_minimal()

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: analysing data multiple samples batches, cells often cluster sample origin rather cell type. happens sample unique technical characteristics (slight differences dissociation, library preparation, sequencing) create systematic biases. Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) fast effective integration method corrects batch effects preserving biological variation. algorithm works follows: Soft clustering: Cells assigned probabilistically multiple clusters PCA space Calculate centroids: cluster, compute centroid separately batch Adjust embeddings: Move cells toward global centroid, removing batch-specific shifts Iterate: Repeat convergence key advantage Harmony operates directly PCA embeddings, making fast memory-efficient. Unlike methods require re-analysis raw counts, Harmony can integrate datasets seconds minutes. Important considerations: -integration: Aggressive correction can merge distinct cell types. check examining marker genes clustering. -integration: Insufficient correction leaves batch effects. verify checking sample mixing UMAP. Biological variation: sample-specific patterns real biology (e.g., disease vs healthy). Harmony preserve removing technical artefacts.
code: # Run Harmony integration # group.by.vars specifies which variable contains batch information # Here we integrate by sample to remove sample-specific technical effects set.seed(42)  # Harmony has stochastic components seu <- RunHarmony(     seu,     group.by.vars = "sample",     reduction.use = "pca",     dims.use = 1:n_dims,     verbose = FALSE )

title: Module 2: Normalisation, Integration & Clustering
text: PCA excellent capturing global structure variance, uses linear projections represent complex, non-linear relationships cells. UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation Projection; McInnes et al., 2018) addresses limitation. UMAP works : Building high-dimensional graph: Connect cell nearest neighbours high-dimensional space (Harmony embeddings) Optimising low-dimensional representation: Find 2D coordinates preserve neighbour relationships much possible Key properties UMAP: Local structure preserved: Cells close original space remain close UMAP Global structure approximate: Distances distant groups less meaningful Clusters appear islands: Distinct cell types typically form separate “islands” UMAP space Important caveats: UMAP primarily visualisation, quantitative analysis size density clusters UMAP reflect number cells -interpret distances clusters run UMAP Harmony-corrected embeddings ensure batch effects distort visualisation:
code: set.seed(42)  # UMAP is stochastic - seed ensures reproducible embeddings seu <- RunUMAP(     seu,     reduction = "harmony",     dims = 1:n_dims,     seed.use = 42,     verbose = FALSE )

title: Module 4: Differential Expression Analysis
text: critical pitfall single cell differential expression analysis pseudoreplication: treating cells independent biological replicates . Cells sample share technical biological variation violates independence assumption statistical tests. Consider analogy: want compare heights two populations, measuring person multiple times increase sample size. Similarly, capturing 5,000 cells one individual give us 5,000 independent observations individual’s biology. Many single cell DE methods (Wilcoxon test, t-test, MAST) operate cell level treat cell independent replicate. approaches: Inflate Type error rates (false positives) dramatically Produce artificially small p-values reflect true significance Confound biological technical variation generalise findings beyond specific samples analysed solution pseudobulk analysis: aggregating counts across cells within sample create sample-level expression estimates, applying well-established bulk RNA-seq methods. approach: Correctly identifies biological replicate (sample/individual) Properly controls false discovery rates Accounts sample--sample variation Produces results generalise population

code: # Function to create contrasts for a cell type create_celltype_contrasts <- function(ct_short, design) {     # Get coefficient names containing this cell type     coefs <- colnames(design)     ct_coefs <- coefs[grep(paste0("^", ct_short, "\\."), coefs)]      if (length(ct_coefs) < 6) {         warning("Insufficient coefficients for ", ct_short)         return(NULL)     }      # Define contrasts averaging over sex     # Young vs Fetal     yvf <- paste0("0.5*(", ct_short, ".young.m + ", ct_short, ".young.f) - ",                   "0.5*(", ct_short, ".fetal.m + ", ct_short, ".fetal.f)")      # Adult vs Fetal     avf <- paste0("0.5*(", ct_short, ".adult.m + ", ct_short, ".adult.f) - ",                   "0.5*(", ct_short, ".fetal.m + ", ct_short, ".fetal.f)")      # Adult vs Young     avy <- paste0("0.5*(", ct_short, ".adult.m + ", ct_short, ".adult.f) - ",                   "0.5*(", ct_short, ".young.m + ", ct_short, ".young.f)")      # Use contrasts parameter (character vector) to avoid scoping issues     contrast_list <- c(yvf, avf, avy)     cm <- makeContrasts(contrasts = contrast_list, levels = design)     # Set proper column names for the contrast matrix     colnames(cm) <- c("YvF", "AvF", "AvY")     cm }

code: # Function to create volcano plot create_volcano <- function(fit_obj, coef_name, title) {     results <- topTreat(fit_obj, coef = coef_name, n = Inf)     results$significant <- results$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & abs(results$logFC) > 0.5      # Label top genes     top_genes <- results %>%         filter(significant) %>%         arrange(adj.P.Val) %>%         head(10)      ggplot(results, aes(x = logFC, y = -log10(adj.P.Val))) +         geom_point(aes(colour = significant), alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +         geom_text(             data = top_genes,             aes(label = SYMBOL),             size = 2.5, hjust = -0.1, vjust = 0.5,             check_overlap = TRUE         ) +         geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.5, 0.5), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +         geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +         scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", "TRUE" = "#D62728")) +         labs(             title = title,             x = "log2 Fold Change",             y = "-log10(adjusted P-value)"         ) +         theme_minimal() +         theme(legend.position = "none") }  # Create volcano plots for Adult vs Fetal across cell types v1 <- create_volcano(treat_cardio, "AvF", "Cardiomyocytes: Adult vs Fetal") v2 <- create_volcano(treat_fibro, "AvF", "Fibroblasts: Adult vs Fetal") v3 <- create_volcano(treat_endo, "AvF", "Endothelial: Adult vs Fetal") v4 <- create_volcano(treat_immune, "AvF", "Immune: Adult vs Fetal")  (v1 + v2) / (v3 + v4) +     plot_annotation(         title = "Volcano Plots: Adult vs Fetal Development",         subtitle = "Dashed lines indicate |logFC| > 0.5 and FDR < 0.05 thresholds"     )
